tactics.name: Model
tactics.definition: The model tactic is used to apply security engineering, vulnerability, threat, and risk analyses to digital systems. This is accomplished by creating and maintaining a common understanding of the systems being defended, the operations on those systems, actors using the systems, and the relationships and interactions between these elements.

tactics.name: Harden
tactics.definition: The harden tactic is used to increase the opportunity cost of computer network exploitation. Hardening differs from Detection in that it generally is conducted before a system is online and operational.

tactics.name: Detect
tactics.definition: The detect tactic is used to identify adversary access to or unauthorized activity on computer networks.

tactics.name: Isolate
tactics.definition: The isolate tactic creates logical or physical barriers in a system which reduces opportunities for adversaries to create further accesses.

tactics.name: Deceive
tactics.definition: The deceive tactic is used to advertise, entice, and allow potential attackers access to an observed or controlled environment.

tactics.name: Evict
tactics.definition: The eviction tactic is used to remove an adversary from a computer network.

tactics.name: Restore
tactics.definition: The restore tactic is used to return the system to a better state.

techniques.name: Operational Activity Mapping
techniques.definition: Operational activity mapping identifies activities of the organization and the organization's suborganizations, groups, roles, and individuals that carry out the activities and then establishes the dependencies of the activities on the systems and people that perform those activities.

techniques.name: Organization Mapping
techniques.definition: Organization mapping identifies and models the people, roles, and groups with an organization and the relations between them.

techniques.name: Operational Risk Assessment
techniques.definition: Operational risk assessment identifies and models the vulnerabilities of, and risks to, an organization's activities individually and as a whole.

techniques.name: Operational Dependency Mapping
techniques.definition: Operational dependency mapping identifies and models the dependencies of the organization's activities on each other and on the organization's performers (people, systems, and services.)  This may include modeling the higher- and lower-level activities of an organization forming a hierarchy, or layering, of the dependencies in an organization's activities.

techniques.name: Access Modeling
techniques.definition: Access modeling captures and records the access permissions granted to identities (e.g., administrators, users, groups, systems) and optionally includes details on how these identities are stored, managed, and shared across systems.

techniques.name: Network Mapping
techniques.definition: Network mapping encompasses the techniques to identify and model the physical layer, network layer, and data exchange layers of the organization's network and their physical location, and determine allowed pathways through that network.

techniques.name: Physical Link Mapping
techniques.definition: Physical link mapping identifies and models the link connectivity of the network devices within a physical network.

techniques.name: Direct Physical Link Mapping
techniques.definition: Direct physical link mapping creates a physical link map by direct observation and recording of the physical network links.

techniques.name: Active Physical Link Mapping
techniques.definition: Active physical link mapping sends and receives network traffic as a means to map the physical layer.

techniques.name: Network Vulnerability Assessment
techniques.definition: Network vulnerability assessment relates all the vulnerabilities of a network's components in the context of their configuration and interdependencies and can also include assessing risk emerging from the network's design as a whole, not just the sum of individual network node or network segment vulnerabilities.

techniques.name: Network Traffic Policy Mapping
techniques.definition: Network traffic policy mapping identifies and models the allowed pathways of data at the network, transport, and/or application levels.

techniques.name: Logical Link Mapping
techniques.definition: Logical link mapping creates a model of existing or previous node-to-node connections using network-layer data or metadata.

techniques.name: Passive Logical Link Mapping
techniques.definition: Passive logical link mapping only listens to network traffic as a means to map the whole data link layer, where the links represent logical data flows rather than physical connections.

techniques.name: Active Logical Link Mapping
techniques.definition: Active logical link mapping sends and receives network traffic as a means to map the whole data link layer, where the links represent logical data flows rather than physical connection

techniques.name: Asset Inventory
techniques.definition: Asset inventorying identifies and records the organization's assets and enriches each inventory item with knowledge about their vulnerabilities.

techniques.name: Software Inventory
techniques.definition: Software inventorying identifies and records the software items in the organization's architecture.

techniques.name: Network Node Inventory
techniques.definition: Network node inventorying identifies and records all the network nodes (hosts, routers, switches, firewalls, etc.) in the organization's architecture.

techniques.name: Hardware Component Inventory
techniques.definition: Hardware component inventorying identifies and records the hardware items in the organization's architecture.

techniques.name: Data Inventory
techniques.definition: Data inventorying identifies and records the schemas, formats, volumes, and locations of data stored and used on the organization's architecture.

techniques.name: Configuration Inventory
techniques.definition: Configuration inventory identifies and records the configuration of software and hardware and their components throughout the organization.

techniques.name: Asset Vulnerability Enumeration
techniques.definition: Asset vulnerability enumeration enriches inventory items with knowledge identifying their vulnerabilities.

techniques.name: Container Image Analysis
techniques.definition: Analyzing a Container Image with respect to a set of policies.

techniques.name: System Mapping
techniques.definition: System mapping encompasses the techniques to identify the organization's systems, how they are configured and decomposed into subsystems and components, how they are dependent on one another, and where they are physically located.

techniques.name: System Vulnerability Assessment
techniques.definition: System vulnerability assessment relates all the vulnerabilities of a system's components in the context of their configuration and internal dependencies and can also include assessing risk emerging from the system's design as a whole, not just the sum of individual component vulnerabilities.

techniques.name: System Dependency Mapping
techniques.definition: System dependency mapping identifies and models the dependencies of system components on each other to carry out their function.

techniques.name: Service Dependency Mapping
techniques.definition: Service dependency mapping determines the services on which each given service relies.

techniques.name: Data Exchange Mapping
techniques.definition: Data exchange mapping identifies and models the organization's intended design for the flows of the data types, formats, and volumes between systems at the application layer.

techniques.name: Source Code Hardening
techniques.definition: Hardening source code with the intention of making it more difficult to exploit and less error prone.

techniques.name: Variable Type Validation
techniques.definition: Ensuring that a variable has the correct type.

techniques.name: Variable Initialization
techniques.definition: Setting variables to a known value before use.

techniques.name: Trusted Library
techniques.definition: A trusted library is a collection of pre-verified and secure code modules or components that are used within software applications to perform specific functions. These libraries are considered reliable and have been vetted for security vulnerabilities, ensuring they do not introduce risks into the application.

techniques.name: Reference Nullification
techniques.definition: Invalidating all pointers that reference a specific memory block, ensuring that the block cannot be accessed or modified after deallocation.

techniques.name: Pointer Validation
techniques.definition: Ensuring that a pointer variable has the required properties for use.

techniques.name: Null Pointer Checking
techniques.definition: Checking if a pointer is NULL.

techniques.name: Memory Block Start Validation
techniques.definition: Ensuring that a pointer accurately references the beginning of a designated memory block.

techniques.name: Integer Range Validation
techniques.definition: Ensuring that an integer is within a valid range.

techniques.name: Domain Logic Validation
techniques.definition: Validation of variable state in the context of the domain application.

techniques.name: Operational Logic Validation
techniques.definition: Validation of variable state in the context of the control logic of the operational application.

techniques.name: Credential Scrubbing
techniques.definition: The systematic removal of hard-coded credentials from source code to prevent accidental exposure and unauthorized access.

techniques.name: Agent Authentication
techniques.definition: Agent authentication is the process of verifying the identities of agents to ensure they are authorized and trustworthy participants within a system.

techniques.name: Token-based Authentication
techniques.definition: Token-based authentication is an authentication protocol where users verify their identity in exchange for a unique access token. Users can then access the website, application, or resource for the life of the token without having to re-enter their credentials.

techniques.name: Password Authentication
techniques.definition: Password authentication is a security mechanism used to verify the identity of a user or entity attempting to access a system or resource by requiring the input of a secret string of characters, known as a password, that is associated with the user or entity.

techniques.name: Multi-factor Authentication
techniques.definition: Requiring proof of two or more pieces of evidence in order to authenticate a user.

techniques.name: Certificate-based Authentication
techniques.definition: Requiring a digital certificate in order to authenticate a user.

techniques.name: Biometric Authentication
techniques.definition: Using biological measures in order to authenticate a user.

techniques.name: Message Hardening
techniques.definition: The application of security controls to user-to-user and system-to-system communications so messages remain confidential, unaltered, and verifiable while resisting injection, replay, and tampering.

techniques.name: Transfer Agent Authentication
techniques.definition: Validating that server components of a messaging infrastructure are authorized to send a particular message.

techniques.name: Message Encryption
techniques.definition: Encrypting a message body using a cryptographic key.

techniques.name: Message Authentication
techniques.definition: Authenticating the sender of a message and ensuring message integrity.

techniques.name: Bus Message Authentication
techniques.definition: Applies cryptographic primitives to individual bus frames to verify the sender's identity and ensure the integrity of the data payload.

techniques.name: Credential Hardening
techniques.definition: Credential Hardening techniques modify system or network properties in order to protect system or network/domain credentials.

techniques.name: Token Binding
techniques.definition: Token binding is a security mechanism used to enhance the protection of tokens, such as cookies or OAuth tokens, by binding them to a specific connection.

techniques.name: Strong Password Policy
techniques.definition: Modifying system configuration to increase password strength.

techniques.name: Change Default Password
techniques.definition: Changing the default password means replacing the factory-set credentials with a strong, unique password before the device is deployed, preventing unauthorized access.

techniques.name: Credential Rotation
techniques.definition: Credential rotation is a security procedure in which authentication credentials, such as passwords, API keys, or certificates, are regularly changed or replaced to minimize the risk of unauthorized access.

techniques.name: Password Rotation
techniques.definition: Password rotation is a security policy that mandates the periodic change of user account passwords to mitigate the risk of unauthorized access due to compromised credentials.

techniques.name: One-time Password
techniques.definition: A one-time password is valid for only one user authentication.

techniques.name: Certificate Rotation
techniques.definition: Certificate rotation involves replacing digital certificates and their private keys to maintain cryptographic integrity and trust, mitigating key compromise risks and ensuring continuous secure communications.

techniques.name: Certificate Pinning
techniques.definition: Persisting either a server's X.509 certificate or their public key and comparing that to server's presented identity to allow for greater client confidence in the remote server's identity for SSL connections.

techniques.name: Platform Hardening
techniques.definition:
Hardening components of a Platform with the intention of making them more difficult to exploit.

Platforms includes components such as:
* BIOS UEFI Subsystems
* Hardware security devices such as Trusted Platform Modules
* Boot process logic or code
* Kernel software components

techniques.name: Radiation Hardening
techniques.definition: Radiation hardening is the process of making electronic components and circuits resistant to damage or malfunction caused by high levels of ionizing radiation.

techniques.name: Electromagnetic Radiation Hardening
techniques.definition: The application of physical and material-level design measures to electronic systems, components, or facilities to reduce their susceptibility to damage or disruption from electromagnetic threats.

techniques.name: RF Shielding
techniques.definition: Adding physical barriers to a platform to prevent undesired radio interference.

techniques.name: Disk Encryption
techniques.definition: Encrypting a hard disk partition to prevent cleartext access to a file system.

techniques.name: TPM Boot Integrity
techniques.definition: Assuring the integrity of a platform by demonstrating that the boot process starts from a trusted combination of hardware and software and continues until the operating system has fully booted and applications are running.  Sometimes called Static Root of Trust Measurement (STRM).

techniques.name: Hardware-based Write Protection
techniques.definition: Physical methods of preventing data from being written to computer storage.

techniques.name: Bootloader Authentication
techniques.definition: Cryptographically authenticating the bootloader software before system boot.

techniques.name: System Configuration Permissions
techniques.definition: Restricting system configuration modifications to a specific user or group of users.

techniques.name: File Encryption
techniques.definition: Encrypting a file using a cryptographic key.

techniques.name: Software Update
techniques.definition: Replacing old software on a computer system component.

techniques.name: Driver Load Integrity Checking
techniques.definition: Ensuring the integrity of drivers loaded during initialization of the operating system.

techniques.name: Physical Enclosure Hardening
techniques.definition: Physical changes to a computer enclosure which reduce the ability for agents or the environment to affect the contained computer system.

techniques.name: Application Hardening
techniques.definition: Application Hardening makes an executable application more resilient to a class of exploits which either introduce new code or execute unwanted existing code. These techniques may be applied at compile-time or on an application binary.

techniques.name: Exception Handler Pointer Validation
techniques.definition: Validates that a referenced exception handler pointer is a valid exception handler.

techniques.name: Application Configuration Hardening
techniques.definition: Modifying an application's configuration to reduce its attack surface.

techniques.name: Disable Remote Access
techniques.definition: Limiting access to a computing device which is not required through or from a non-organization-controlled network.

techniques.name: Pointer Authentication
techniques.definition: Comparing the cryptographic hash or derivative of a pointer's value to an expected value.

techniques.name: Dead Code Elimination
techniques.definition: Removing unreachable or "dead code" from compiled source code.

techniques.name: Process Segment Execution Prevention
techniques.definition: Preventing execution of any address in a memory region other than the code segment.

techniques.name: Segment Address Offset Randomization
techniques.definition: Randomizing the base (start) address of one or more segments of memory during the initialization of a process.

techniques.name: Stack Frame Canary Validation
techniques.definition: Comparing a value stored in a stack frame with a known good value in order to prevent or detect a memory segment overwrite.

techniques.name: Control Flow Integrity
techniques.definition: Enforcing legal control flow transfers during application process execution.

techniques.name: Network Traffic Analysis
techniques.definition: Analyzing intercepted or summarized computer network traffic to detect unauthorized activity.

techniques.name: RPC Traffic Analysis
techniques.definition: Monitoring the activity of remote procedure calls in communication traffic to establish standard protocol operations and potential attacker activities.

techniques.name: IPC Traffic Analysis
techniques.definition: Analyzing standard inter process communication (IPC) protocols to detect deviations from normal protocol activity.

techniques.name: Remote Terminal Session Detection
techniques.definition: Detection of an unauthorized remote live terminal console session by examining network traffic to a network host.

techniques.name: Relay Pattern Analysis
techniques.definition: The detection of an internal host relaying traffic between the internal network and the external network.

techniques.name: Protocol Metadata Anomaly Detection
techniques.definition: Collecting network communication protocol metadata and identifying statistical outliers.

techniques.name: Per Host Download-Upload Ratio Analysis
techniques.definition: Detecting anomalies that indicate malicious activity by comparing the amount of data downloaded versus data uploaded by a host.

techniques.name: DNS Traffic Analysis
techniques.definition: Analysis of domain name metadata, including name and DNS records, to determine whether the domain is likely to resolve to an undesirable host.

techniques.name: File Carving
techniques.definition: Identifying and extracting files from network application protocols through the use of network stream reassembly software.

techniques.name: Application Protocol Command Analysis
techniques.definition: Analyzing application protocol level remote commands to detect unauthorized activity.

techniques.name: Remote Firmware Update Monitoring
techniques.definition: Monitoring of remote firmware update commands to identify unauthorized software installations.

techniques.name: Inbound Session Volume Analysis
techniques.definition: Analyzing inbound network session or connection attempt volume.

techniques.name: Network Traffic Community Deviation
techniques.definition: Establishing baseline communities of network hosts and identifying statistically divergent inter-community communication.

techniques.name: Client-server Payload Profiling
techniques.definition: Comparing client-server request and response payloads to a baseline profile to identify outliers.

techniques.name: Administrative Network Activity Analysis
techniques.definition: Detection of unauthorized use of administrative network protocols by analyzing network activity against a baseline.

techniques.name: Connection Attempt Analysis
techniques.definition: Analyzing failed connections in a network to detect unauthorized activity.

techniques.name: Network Traffic Signature Analysis
techniques.definition: Analyzing network traffic and compares it to known signatures

techniques.name: Byte Sequence Emulation
techniques.definition: Analyzing sequences of bytes and determining if they likely represent malicious shellcode.

techniques.name: Certificate Analysis
techniques.definition: Analyzing Public Key Infrastructure certificates to detect if they have been misconfigured or spoofed using both network traffic, certificate fields and third-party logs.

techniques.name: Passive Certificate Analysis
techniques.definition: Collecting host certificates from network traffic or other passive sources like a certificate transparency log and analyzing them for unauthorized activity.

techniques.name: Active Certificate Analysis
techniques.definition: Actively collecting PKI certificates by connecting to the server and downloading its server certificates for analysis.

techniques.name: Message Analysis
techniques.definition: Analyzing email or instant message content to detect unauthorized activity.

techniques.name: Sender Reputation Analysis
techniques.definition: Ascertaining sender reputation based on information associated with a message (e.g. email/instant messaging).

techniques.name: Sender MTA Reputation Analysis
techniques.definition: Characterizing the reputation of mail transfer agents (MTA) to determine the security risk in emails.

techniques.name: Process Analysis
techniques.definition: Process Analysis consists of observing a running application process and analyzing it to watch for certain behaviors or conditions which may indicate adversary activity. Analysis can occur inside of the process or through a third-party monitoring application. Examples include monitoring system and privileged calls, monitoring process initiation chains, and memory boundary allocations.

techniques.name: File Access Pattern Analysis
techniques.definition: Analyzing the files accessed by a process to identify unauthorized activity.

techniques.name: Database Query String Analysis
techniques.definition: Analyzing database queries to detect [SQL Injection](https://capec.mitre.org/data/definitions/66.html).

techniques.name: Shadow Stack Comparisons
techniques.definition: Comparing a call stack in system memory with a shadow call stack maintained by the processor to determine unauthorized shellcode activity.

techniques.name: Script Execution Analysis
techniques.definition: Analyzing the execution of a script to detect unauthorized user activity.

techniques.name: Process Spawn Analysis
techniques.definition: Analyzing spawn arguments or attributes of a process to detect processes that are unauthorized.

techniques.name: Process Lineage Analysis
techniques.definition: Identification of suspicious processes executing on an end-point device by examining the ancestry and siblings of a process, and the associated metadata of each node on the tree, such as process execution, duration, and order relative to siblings and ancestors.

techniques.name: Indirect Branch Call Analysis
techniques.definition: Analyzing vendor specific branch call recording in order to detect ROP style attacks.

techniques.name: System Call Analysis
techniques.definition: Analyzing system calls to determine whether a process is exhibiting unauthorized behavior.

techniques.name: File Creation Analysis
techniques.definition: Analyzing the properties of file create system call invocations.

techniques.name: Process Self-Modification Detection
techniques.definition: Detects processes that modify, change, or replace their own code at runtime.

techniques.name: Process Code Segment Verification
techniques.definition: Comparing the "text" or "code" memory segments to a source of truth.

techniques.name: Physical Access Monitoring
techniques.definition: Monitoring the physical access of a specified environment through detection, recording, reviewing, and logging of who/what enters and exists areas.

techniques.name: Video Surveillance
techniques.definition: Monitoring of physical areas via camera video feeds to deter, detect, and investigate unauthorized access and related security events.

techniques.name: Proximity Sensor Monitoring
techniques.definition: Monitoring events from proximity sensors that indicate a credential or tagged asset is within the sensor’s read range or a defined zone. Common enabling technologies include RFID, Bluetooth Low Energy (BLE), and Ultra-Wideband (UWB).

techniques.name: Motion Sensor Monitoring
techniques.definition: Monitoring events from motion detectors (e.g., passive IR, microwave, dual-technology) to detect presence or movement within protected areas.

techniques.name: Electronic Lock Monitoring
techniques.definition: Monitoring electronic lock and door hardware states and access events (e.g., locked/unlocked, access granted/denied, door forced/held, tamper) to detect and respond to unauthorized entry.

techniques.name: File Analysis
techniques.definition: File Analysis is an analytic process to determine a file's status. For example: virus, trojan, benign, malicious, trusted, unauthorized, sensitive, etc.

techniques.name: File Hashing
techniques.definition: Employing file hash comparisons to detect known malware.

techniques.name: File Content Analysis
techniques.definition: Employing a pattern matching algorithm to statically analyze the content of files.

techniques.name: File Content Rules
techniques.definition: Employing a pattern matching rule language to analyze the content of files.

techniques.name: Emulated File Analysis
techniques.definition: Emulating instructions in a file looking for specific patterns.

techniques.name: Dynamic Analysis
techniques.definition: Executing or opening a file in a synthetic "sandbox" environment to determine if the file is a malicious program or if the file exploits another program such as a document reader.

techniques.name: User Behavior Analysis
techniques.definition: User behavior analytics ("UBA") as defined by Gartner, is a cybersecurity process about detection of insider threats, targeted attacks, and financial fraud. UBA solutions look at patterns of human behavior, and then apply algorithms and statistical analysis to detect meaningful anomalies from those patterns-anomalies that indicate potential threats.' Instead of tracking devices or security events, UBA tracks a system's users. Big data platforms are increasing UBA functionality by allowing them to analyze petabytes worth of data to detect insider threats and advanced persistent threats.

techniques.name: Domain Account Monitoring
techniques.definition: Monitoring the existence of or changes to Domain User Accounts.

techniques.name: Session Duration Analysis
techniques.definition: Analyzing the duration of user sessions in order to detect unauthorized  activity.

techniques.name: User Geolocation Logon Pattern Analysis
techniques.definition: Monitoring geolocation data of user logon attempts and comparing it to a baseline user behavior profile to identify anomalies in logon location.

techniques.name: Web Session Activity Analysis
techniques.definition: Monitoring changes in user web session behavior by comparing current web session activity to a baseline behavior profile or a catalog of predetermined malicious behavior.

techniques.name: Job Function Access Pattern Analysis
techniques.definition: Detecting anomalies in user access patterns by comparing user access activity to behavioral profiles that categorize users by role such as job title, function, department.

techniques.name: Credential Compromise Scope Analysis
techniques.definition: Determining which credentials may have been compromised by analyzing the user logon history of a particular system.

techniques.name: Authorization Event Thresholding
techniques.definition: Collecting authorization events, creating a baseline user profile, and determining whether authorization events are consistent with the baseline profile.

techniques.name: Authentication Event Thresholding
techniques.definition: Collecting authentication events, creating a baseline user profile, and determining whether authentication events are consistent with the baseline profile.

techniques.name: Resource Access Pattern Analysis
techniques.definition: Analyzing the resources accessed by a user to identify unauthorized activity.

techniques.name: Local Account Monitoring
techniques.definition: Analyzing local user accounts to detect unauthorized activity.

techniques.name: User Data Transfer Analysis
techniques.definition: Analyzing the amount of data transferred by a user.

techniques.name: Identifier Analysis
techniques.definition: Analyzing identifier artifacts such as IP address, domain names, or URL(I)s.

techniques.name: URL Analysis
techniques.definition: Determining if a URL is benign or malicious by analyzing the URL or its components.

techniques.name: Identifier Reputation Analysis
techniques.definition: Analyzing the reputation of an identifier.

techniques.name: URL Reputation Analysis
techniques.definition: Analyzing the reputation of a URL.

techniques.name: IP Reputation Analysis
techniques.definition: Analyzing the reputation of an IP address.

techniques.name: File Hash Reputation Analysis
techniques.definition: Analyzing the reputation of a file hash.

techniques.name: Domain Name Reputation Analysis
techniques.definition: Analyzing the reputation of a domain name.

techniques.name: Identifier Activity Analysis
techniques.definition: Taking known malicious identifiers and determining if they are present in a system.

techniques.name: Homoglyph Detection
techniques.definition: Comparing strings using a variety of techniques to determine if a deceptive or malicious string is being presented to a user.

techniques.name: Platform Monitoring
techniques.definition: Monitoring platform components such as operating systems software, hardware devices, or firmware.

techniques.name: Firmware Embedded Monitoring Code
techniques.definition: Monitoring code is injected into firmware for integrity monitoring of firmware and firmware data.

techniques.name: Application Performance Monitoring
techniques.definition: Monitoring the count and duration of the application or program cycle.

techniques.name: Application Exception Monitoring
techniques.definition: Monitoring the failures of system counters and timers.

techniques.name: Operating System Monitoring
techniques.definition: The operating system software, for D3FEND's purposes, includes the kernel and its process management functions, hardware drivers, initialization or boot logic. It also includes and other key system daemons and their configuration. The monitoring or analysis of these components for unauthorized activity constitute **Operating System Monitoring**.

techniques.name: User Session Init Config Analysis
techniques.definition: Analyzing modifications to user session config files such as .bashrc or .bash_profile.

techniques.name: System Init Config Analysis
techniques.definition: Analysis of any system process startup configuration.

techniques.name: System File Analysis
techniques.definition: Monitoring system files such as authentication databases, configuration files, system logs, and system executables for modification or tampering.

techniques.name: Service Binary Verification
techniques.definition: Analyzing changes in service binary files by comparing to a source of truth.

techniques.name: System Daemon Monitoring
techniques.definition: Tracking changes to the state or configuration of critical system level processes.

techniques.name: Scheduled Job Analysis
techniques.definition: Analysis of source files, processes, destination files, or destination servers associated with a scheduled job to detect unauthorized use of job scheduling.

techniques.name: Memory Boundary Tracking
techniques.definition: Analyzing a call stack for return addresses which point to unexpected  memory locations.

techniques.name: Input Device Analysis
techniques.definition: Operating system level mechanisms to prevent abusive input device exploitation.

techniques.name: Endpoint Health Beacon
techniques.definition: Monitoring the security status of an endpoint by sending periodic messages with health status, where absence of a response may indicate that the endpoint has been compromised.

techniques.name: Platform Uptime Monitoring
techniques.definition: Monitor the amount of time since the last power cycle or restart.

techniques.name: Operational Process Monitoring
techniques.definition: Monitoring physical parameters and operator actions related to an operational environment.

techniques.name: Firmware Verification
techniques.definition: Cryptographically verifying firmware integrity.

techniques.name: System Firmware Verification
techniques.definition: Cryptographically verifying installed system firmware integrity.

techniques.name: Peripheral Firmware Verification
techniques.definition: Cryptographically verifying peripheral firmware integrity.

techniques.name: Firmware Behavior Analysis
techniques.definition: Analyzing the behavior of embedded code in firmware and looking for anomalous behavior and suspicious activity.

techniques.name: File Integrity Monitoring
techniques.definition: Detecting any suspicious changes to files in a computer system.

techniques.name: Operating Mode Monitoring
techniques.definition: Detects operating modes such as Program, Run, Remote, or Stop.

techniques.name: Access Mediation
techniques.definition: Access mediation is the process of granting or denying specific requests to: 1) obtain and use information and related information processing services; and 2) enter specific physical facilities (e.g., Federal buildings, military establishments, border crossing entrances). Access mediation decisions should enforce least privilege by granting access for scoped durations to prevent privilege creep and, where applicable, implement just-in-time (JIT) access. Denial decisions may prevent initial access or terminate access that has already been granted, ensuring continuous enforcement of security policies.

techniques.name: System Call Filtering
techniques.definition: Controlling access to local computer system resources with kernel-level capabilities.

techniques.name: Local File Access Mediation
techniques.definition: Local file access mediation is the process of an operating system granting or denying a specific access request to a local file.

techniques.name: Physical Access Mediation
techniques.definition: Physical access mediation is the process of granting or denying specific requests to enter specific physical facilities (e.g., Federal buildings, military establishments, border crossing entrances.)

techniques.name: Physical Locking
techniques.definition: Employ a mechanical locking device for securing moveable portions of physical barriers (e.g., doors, gates, drawers) in a secured position.

techniques.name: Operating Mode Restriction
techniques.definition: Restricting unauthorized changes to the operating mode prevents devices from switching into inappropriate or vulnerable states during normal use.

techniques.name: OT Variable Access Restriction
techniques.definition: Assign read/write access controls on designated registers or data tags to prevent unauthorized writes.

techniques.name: Network Resource Access Mediation
techniques.definition: Control of access to organizational systems and services by users or processes over a network.

techniques.name: Web Session Access Mediation
techniques.definition: Web session access mediation secures user sessions in web applications by employing robust authentication and integrity validation, along with adaptive threat mitigation techniques, to ensure that access to web resources is authorized and protected from session-related attacks.

techniques.name: Proxy-based Web Server Access Mediation
techniques.definition: Proxy-based web server access mediation focuses on the regulation of web server access through intermediary proxy servers.

techniques.name: Endpoint-based Web Server Access Mediation
techniques.definition: Endpoint-based web server access mediation regulates web server access directly from user endpoints by implementing mechanisms such as client-side certificates and endpoint security software to authenticate devices and ensure compliant access.

techniques.name: Remote File Access Mediation
techniques.definition: Remote file access mediation is the process of managing and securing access to file systems over a network to ensure that only authorized users or processes can interact with remote files.

techniques.name: Network Access Mediation
techniques.definition: Network access mediation is the control method for authorizing access to a system by a user (or a process acting on behalf of a user) communicating through a network, including a local area network, a wide area network, and the Internet.

techniques.name: Routing Access Mediation
techniques.definition: Routing access mediation is a network security approach that manages and controls access at the network layer using VPNs, tunneling protocols, firewall rules, and traffic inspection to ensure secure and efficient data routing.

techniques.name: LAN Access Mediation
techniques.definition: LAN access mediation encompasses the application of strict access control policies, systematic verification of devices, and authentication mechanisms to govern connectivity to a Local Area Network.

techniques.name: IO Port Restriction
techniques.definition: Limiting access to computer input/output (IO) ports to restrict unauthorized devices.

techniques.name: Credential Transmission Scoping
techniques.definition: Limiting the transmission of a credential to a scoped set of relying parties.

techniques.name: Content Filtering
techniques.definition: Content Filtering techniques aid in the process of analyzing an input file for malicious or erroneous content and outputting a sanitized version.

techniques.name: Content Validation
techniques.definition: Verify and validate contents complies with policy

techniques.name: File Format Verification
techniques.definition: Verifying that a file conforms to its expected format specifications

techniques.name: File Metadata Value Verification
techniques.definition: The process of checking specific static values within a file, such as file signatures or magic numbers, to ensure they match the expected values defined by the file format specification.

techniques.name: File Magic Byte Verification
techniques.definition: Utilizing the magic number to verify the file

techniques.name: File Metadata Consistency Validation
techniques.definition: The process of validating the consistency between a file's metadata and its actual content, ensuring that elements like declared lengths, pointers, and checksums accurately describe the file's content.

techniques.name: File Internal Structure Verification
techniques.definition: The process of checking specific static values within a file, such as file signatures or magic numbers, to ensure they match the expected values defined by the file format specification.

techniques.name: File Content Decompression Checking
techniques.definition: Checking if compressed or encoded data sections can be successfully decompressed or decoded. Can follow with further analysis with semantic knowledge

techniques.name: Content Quarantine
techniques.definition: Transfer content that does not comply with policy to a quarantine zone.

techniques.name: Content Modification
techniques.definition: Modify content that does not comply with policy.

techniques.name: Content Substitution
techniques.definition: Modifies specific digital content information by replacing it with something else.

techniques.name: Content Rebuild
techniques.definition: Rebuild the file according to the spec so any unreferenced components or objects are removed.

techniques.name: Content Format Conversion
techniques.definition: Content format conversion is mechanical transformation from one format to another which may be normalization or specifically flattening.

techniques.name: Content Excision
techniques.definition: Removing specific, potentially malicious, parts of content

techniques.name: Execution Isolation
techniques.definition: Execution Isolation techniques prevent application processes from accessing non-essential system resources, such as memory, devices, or files.

techniques.name: Kernel-based Process Isolation
techniques.definition: Using kernel-level capabilities to isolate processes.

techniques.name: Hardware-based Process Isolation
techniques.definition: Preventing one process from writing to the memory space of another process through hardware based address manager implementations.

techniques.name: Executable Denylisting
techniques.definition: Blocking the execution of files on a host in accordance with defined application policy rules.

techniques.name: Executable Allowlisting
techniques.definition: Using a digital signature to authenticate a file before opening.

techniques.name: Application-based Process Isolation
techniques.definition: Application code which prevents its own subroutines from accessing intra-process / internal memory space.

techniques.name: Access Policy Administration
techniques.definition: Access policy administration is the systematic process of defining, implementing, and managing access control policies that dictate user permissions to resources.

techniques.name: User Group Permissions
techniques.definition: Access control where access is determined based on attributes associated with users and the objects being accessed.

techniques.name: User Account Permissions
techniques.definition: Restricting a user account's access to resources.

techniques.name: Local File Permissions
techniques.definition: Local file permissions is the systematic process of defining, implementing, and managing access control policies that dictate user permissions for accessing files on a local system through the configuration of operating system functionality.

techniques.name: Domain Trust Policy
techniques.definition: Restricting inter-domain trust by modifying domain configuration.

techniques.name: Network Isolation
techniques.definition: Network Isolation techniques prevent network hosts from accessing non-essential system network resources.

techniques.name: Network Traffic Filtering
techniques.definition: Restricting network traffic originating from any location.

techniques.name: Outbound Traffic Filtering
techniques.definition: Restricting network traffic originating from a private host or enclave destined towards untrusted networks.

techniques.name: Inbound Traffic Filtering
techniques.definition: Restricting network traffic originating from untrusted networks destined towards a private host or enclave.

techniques.name: Email Filtering
techniques.definition: Filtering incoming email traffic based on specific criteria.

techniques.name: Encrypted Tunnels
techniques.definition: Encrypted encapsulation of routable network traffic.

techniques.name: Directional Network Link
techniques.definition: Enforce one-way network communication by preventing two-way communication.

techniques.name: DNS Denylisting
techniques.definition: Blocking DNS Network Traffic based on criteria such as IP address, domain name, or DNS query type.

techniques.name: Reverse Resolution IP Denylisting
techniques.definition: Blocking a reverse lookup based on the query's IP address value.

techniques.name: Forward Resolution IP Denylisting
techniques.definition: Blocking a DNS lookup's answer's IP address value.

techniques.name: Forward Resolution Domain Denylisting
techniques.definition: Blocking a lookup based on the query's domain name value.

techniques.name: Homoglyph Denylisting
techniques.definition: Blocking DNS queries that are deceptively similar to legitimate domain names.

techniques.name: Hierarchical Domain Denylisting
techniques.definition: Blocking the resolution of any subdomain of a specified domain name.

techniques.name: DNS Allowlisting
techniques.definition: Permitting only approved domains and their subdomains to be resolved.

techniques.name: Broadcast Domain Isolation
techniques.definition: Broadcast isolation restricts the number of computers a host can contact on their LAN.

techniques.name: Decoy Object
techniques.definition: A Decoy Object is created and deployed for the purposes of deceiving attackers.

techniques.name: Decoy User Credential
techniques.definition: A Credential created for the purpose of deceiving an adversary.

techniques.name: Decoy Session Token
techniques.definition: An authentication token created for the purposes of deceiving an adversary.

techniques.name: Decoy Public Release
techniques.definition: Issuing publicly released media to deceive adversaries.

techniques.name: Decoy Persona
techniques.definition: Establishing a fake online identity to misdirect, deceive, and or interact with adversaries.

techniques.name: Decoy Network Resource
techniques.definition: Deploying a network resource for the purposes of deceiving an adversary.

techniques.name: Decoy File
techniques.definition: A file created for the purposes of deceiving an adversary.

techniques.name: Decoy Environment
techniques.definition: A Decoy Environment comprises hosts and networks for the purposes of deceiving an attacker.

techniques.name: Standalone Honeynet
techniques.definition: An environment created for the purpose of attracting attackers and eliciting their behaviors that is not connected to any production enterprise systems.

techniques.name: Integrated Honeynet
techniques.definition: The practice of setting decoys in a production environment to entice interaction from attackers.

techniques.name: Connected Honeynet
techniques.definition: A decoy service, system, or environment, that is connected to the enterprise network, and simulates or emulates certain functionality to the network, without exposing full access to a production system.

techniques.name: Process Eviction
techniques.definition: Process eviction techniques terminate or remove running process.

techniques.name: Session Termination
techniques.definition: Forcefully end all active sessions associated with compromised accounts or devices.

techniques.name: Process Termination
techniques.definition: Terminating a running application process on a computer system.

techniques.name: Process Suspension
techniques.definition: Suspending a running process on a computer system.

techniques.name: Host Shutdown
techniques.definition: Initiating a host's shutdown sequence to terminate all running processes.

techniques.name: Host Reboot
techniques.definition: Initiating a host's reboot sequence to terminate all running processes.

techniques.name: Object Eviction
techniques.definition: Terminate or remove an object from a host machine. This is the broadest class for object eviction.

techniques.name: Registry Key Deletion
techniques.definition: Delete a registry key.

techniques.name: File Eviction
techniques.definition: File eviction techniques delete files from system storage.

techniques.name: Email Removal
techniques.definition: The email removal technique deletes email files from system storage.

techniques.name: Domain Registration Takedown
techniques.definition: The process of performing a takedown of the attacker's domain registration infrastructure.

techniques.name: Disk Formatting
techniques.definition: Disk Formatting is the process of preparing a data storage device, such as a hard drive, solid-state drive, or USB flash drive, for initial use.

techniques.name: Disk Partitioning
techniques.definition: Disk Partitioning is the process of dividing a disk into multiple distinct sections, known as partitions.

techniques.name: Disk Erasure
techniques.definition: Disk Erasure is the process of securely deleting all data on a disk to ensure that it cannot be recovered by any means.

techniques.name: DNS Cache Eviction
techniques.definition: Flushing DNS to clear any IP addresses or other DNS records from the cache.

techniques.name: Credential Eviction
techniques.definition: Credential Eviction techniques disable or remove compromised credentials from a computer network.

techniques.name: Credential Revocation
techniques.definition: Deleting a set of credentials permanently to prevent them from being used to authenticate.

techniques.name: Authentication Cache Invalidation
techniques.definition: Removing tokens or credentials from an authentication cache to prevent further user associated account accesses.

techniques.name: Account Locking
techniques.definition: The process of temporarily disabling user accounts on a system or domain.

techniques.name: Restore Object
techniques.definition: Restoring an object for an entity to access. This is the broadest class for object restoral.

techniques.name: Restore Software
techniques.definition: Restoring software to a host.

techniques.name: Restore File
techniques.definition: Restoring a file for an entity to access.

techniques.name: Restore Email
techniques.definition: Restoring an email for an entity to access.

techniques.name: Restore Disk Image
techniques.definition: Restoring a previously captured disk image a hard drive.

techniques.name: Restore Database
techniques.definition: Restoring the data in a database.

techniques.name: Restore Configuration
techniques.definition: Restoring an software configuration.

techniques.name: Restore Access
techniques.definition: Restoring an entity's access to resources.

techniques.name: Restore User Account Access
techniques.definition: Restoring a user account's access to resources.

techniques.name: Unlock Account
techniques.definition: Restoring a user account's access to resources by unlocking a locked User Account.

techniques.name: Restore Network Access
techniques.definition: Restoring a entity's access to a computer network.

techniques.name: Reissue Credential
techniques.definition: Issue a new credential to a user which supersedes their old credential.

artifacts.name: Dependency
artifacts.definition: A dependency is the relationship of relying on or being controlled by someone or something else.  This class reifies dependencies that correspond to the object property depends-on.

artifacts.name: Organization
artifacts.definition: An organization with a defined mission/goal and a defined boundary, using systems to execute that mission, and with responsibility for managing its own risks and performance. An enterprise may consist of all or some of the following business aspects: acquisition, program management, human resources, financial management, security, and systems, information and mission management

artifacts.name: Person
artifacts.definition: A person is a human being.

artifacts.name: Operational Activity Plan
artifacts.definition: An activity is a specific behavior representing a set of actions that may be accomplished by an agent.

artifacts.name: Vulnerability
artifacts.definition: A Vulnerability is a publicly disclosed instance of one or more weaknesses in a product that an attacker could exploit, violating its confidentiality, integrity, or availability.

artifacts.name: Access Control Configuration
artifacts.definition: Information about what access permissions are granted to particular users for particular objects.

artifacts.name: Digital Identity
artifacts.definition: The unique representation of a subject engaged in an online transaction. A digital identity is always unique in the context of a digital service, but does not necessarily need to uniquely identify the subject in all contexts. In other words, accessing a digital service may not mean that the subject's real-life identity is known.  Note: There is no single, widely accepted definition for this term and context is important. This definition is specific to online transactions.

artifacts.name: User Account
artifacts.definition: A user account allows a user to authenticate to a system and potentially to receive authorization to access resources provided by or connected to that system; however, authentication does not imply authorization. To log into an account, a user is typically required to authenticate oneself with a password or other credentials for the purposes of accounting, security, logging, and resource management.

artifacts.name: Network Node
artifacts.definition: In telecommunications networks, a node (Latin nodus, 'knot') is either a redistribution point or a communication endpoint. The definition of a node depends on the network and protocol layer referred to. A physical network node is an electronic device that is attached to a network, and is capable of creating, receiving, or transmitting information over a communications channel. A passive distribution point such as a distribution frame or patch panel is consequently not a node.

artifacts.name: Physical Link
artifacts.definition:
A physical link is a dedicated connection for communication that uses some physical media (electrical, electromagnetic, optical, to include clear spaces or vacuums.)  A physical link represents only a single hop (link) in any larger communications path, circuit, or network.

NOTE: not synonymous with data link as a data link can be over a telecommunications circuit, which may be a virtual circuit composed of multiple physical links.

artifacts.name: Network Agent
artifacts.definition: A network agent is software installed on a network node or device that transmits information back to a collector agent or management system.  Kinds of network agents include SNMP Agent, IPMI agents, WBEM agents, and many proprietary agents capturing network monitoring and management information.

artifacts.name: Network
artifacts.definition: A network is a group of computers that use a set of common communication protocols over digital interconnections for the purpose of sharing resources located on or provided by the network nodes. The interconnections between nodes are formed from a broad spectrum of telecommunication network technologies, based on physically wired, optical, and wireless radio-frequency methods that may be arranged in a variety of network topologies.

artifacts.name: Logical Link
artifacts.definition: A Logical Link is an abstract or virtual connection between two entities that facilitates communication or data exchange without requiring a direct physical connection.

artifacts.name: Software
artifacts.definition: Computer software, or simply software, is that part of a computer system that consists of encoded information or computer instructions, in contrast to the physical hardware from which the system is built.

artifacts.name: Hardware Device
artifacts.definition: Hardware devices are the physical artifacts that constitute a network or computer system. Hardware devices are the physical parts or components of a computer, such as the monitor, keyboard, computer data storage, hard disk drive (HDD), graphic cards, sound cards, memory (RAM), motherboard, and so on, all of which are tangible physical objects. By contrast, software is instructions that can be stored and run by hardware. Hardware is directed by the software to execute any command or instruction. A combination of hardware and software forms a usable computing system.

artifacts.name: Database
artifacts.definition: A database is an organized collection of data, generally stored and accessed electronically from a computer system. Where databases are more complex they are often developed using formal design and modeling techniques.

artifacts.name: Document File
artifacts.definition: A document is a written, drawn, presented or recorded representation of thoughts. An electronic document file is usually used to describe a primarily textual file, along with its structure and design, such as fonts, colors and additional images.

artifacts.name: Configuration Resource
artifacts.definition: A resource used to configure a system including software and hardware.

artifacts.name: Container Image
artifacts.definition:
A container is a standard unit of software that packages up code and all its dependencies so the application runs quickly and reliably from one computing environment to another. A Docker container image is a lightweight, standalone, executable package of software that includes everything needed to run an application: code, runtime, system tools, system libraries and settings.

Container images become containers at runtime and in the case of Docker containers - images become containers when they run on Docker Engine. Available for both Linux and Windows-based applications, containerized software will always run the same, regardless of the infrastructure. Containers isolate software from its environment and ensure that it works uniformly despite differences for instance between development and staging.

artifacts.name: Digital System
artifacts.definition: A digital system is a group of interacting or interrelated digital artifacts that act according to a set of rules to form a unified whole. A digital system, surrounded and influenced by its environment, is described by its boundaries, structure and purpose and expressed in its functioning. Systems are the subjects of study of systems theory.

artifacts.name: System Dependency
artifacts.definition: A system dependency indicates a system has an activity, agent, or another system which relies on it in order to be functional.

artifacts.name: Service Dependency
artifacts.definition: A service dependency indicates a service has an activity, agent, or another service which relies on it in order to be functional.

artifacts.name: Data Dependency
artifacts.definition: A Data Dependency exists when a process, operation, or system requires specific data in order to execute correctly.

artifacts.name: Pointer Dereferencing Function
artifacts.definition: A function which has an operation which dereferences a pointer.

artifacts.name: Subroutine
artifacts.definition: In different programming languages, a subroutine may be called a procedure, a function, a routine, a method, or a subprogram. The generic term callable unit is sometimes used.

artifacts.name: Memory Free Function
artifacts.definition: Releases previously reserved memory associated with a process.

artifacts.name: Mathematical Function
artifacts.definition: Computes mathematical expressions.

artifacts.name: OT Control Function
artifacts.definition: A function which accesses OT Control Variables

artifacts.name: Agent
artifacts.definition: An entity capable of performing intentional actions.

artifacts.name: Access Token
artifacts.definition: In computer systems, an access token contains the security credentials for a login session and identifies the user, the user's groups, the user's privileges, and, in some cases, a particular application. Typically one may be asked to enter the access token (e.g. 40 random characters) rather than the usual password (it therefore should be kept secret just like a password).

artifacts.name: Password
artifacts.definition: A password, sometimes called a passcode, is a memorized secret, typically a string of characters, usually used to confirm the identity of a user. Using the terminology of the NIST Digital Identity Guidelines, the secret is memorized by a party called the claimant while the party verifying the identity of the claimant is called the verifier. When the claimant successfully demonstrates knowledge of the password to the verifier through an established authentication protocol, the verifier is able to infer the claimant's identity.

artifacts.name: Credential
artifacts.definition: A credential is a physical/tangible object, a piece of knowledge, or a facet of a person's physical being that enables an individual access to a given physical facility or computer-based information system. Typically, credentials can be something a person knows (such as a number or PIN), something they have (such as an access badge), something they are (such as a biometric feature), something they do (measurable behavioral patterns) or some combination of these items. This is known as multi-factor authentication. The typical credential is an access card or key-fob, and newer software can also turn users' smartphones into access devices.

artifacts.name: Certificate
artifacts.definition: In cryptography, a public key certificate, also known as a digital certificate or identity certificate, is an electronic document used to prove the ownership of a public key. The certificate includes information about the key, information about the identity of its owner (called the subject), and the digital signature of an entity that has verified the certificate's contents (called the issuer). If the signature is valid, and the software examining the certificate trusts the issuer, then it can use that key to communicate securely with the certificate's subject. In email encryption, code signing, and e-signature systems, a certificate's subject is typically a person or organization. However, in Transport Layer Security (TLS) a certificate's subject is typically a computer or other device.

artifacts.name: Digital Message
artifacts.definition: A discrete unit of digital communication created by a sender for one or more intended recipients. Encoded in an application-layer format, a digital message conveys semantics such as commands, data, or status and is transported inside lower-layer containers like network frames or packets.

artifacts.name: Bus Message
artifacts.definition: A digital message potentially containing commands, telemetry, or status signals, encoded in a bus protocol and conveyed over a bus within one or more frames.

artifacts.name: OT Controller
artifacts.definition: An OT Controller is an industrial control device that automatically regulates one or more controlled variables in response to command inputs and real-time feedback signals.

artifacts.name: Public Key
artifacts.definition: A public key can be disseminated widely as part of an asymmetric cryptography framework and be used to encrypt messages to send to the public key's owner or to authenticate signed messages from that sender.

artifacts.name: Storage
artifacts.definition: Computer data storage, often called storage or memory, is a technology consisting of computer components and recording media used to retain digital data. It is a core function and fundamental component of computers. In the Von Neumann architecture, the CPU consists of two main parts: The control unit and the arithmetic / logic unit (ALU). The former controls the flow of data between the CPU and memory, while the latter performs arithmetic and logical operations on data.

artifacts.name: Secondary Storage
artifacts.definition: Secondary memory (storage, hard disk) is the computer component holding information that does not need to be accessed quickly and that needs to be retained long-term.

artifacts.name: Boot Loader
artifacts.definition: A bootloader is software that is responsible for booting a computer. When a computer is turned off, its software‍-‌including operating systems, application code, and data‍-‌remains stored on non-volatile memory. When the computer is powered on, it typically does not have an operating system or its loader in random-access memory (RAM). The computer first executes a relatively small program stored in read-only memory (ROM, and later EEPROM, NOR flash) along with some needed data, to initialize RAM (especially on x86 systems) to access the nonvolatile device (usually block device, eg NAND flash) or devices from which the operating system programs and data can be loaded into RAM.

artifacts.name: System Configuration Database
artifacts.definition: A database used to hold system configuration data.

artifacts.name: File
artifacts.definition: A file maintained in computer-readable form.

artifacts.name: Hardware Driver
artifacts.definition: In computing, a device driver (commonly referred to simply as a driver) is a computer program that operates or controls a particular type of device that is attached to a computer. A driver provides a software interface to hardware devices, enabling operating systems and other computer programs to access hardware functions without needing to know precise details of the hardware being used. A driver communicates with the device through the computer bus or communications subsystem to which the hardware connects. When a calling program invokes a routine in the driver, the driver issues commands to the device. Once the device sends data back to the driver, the driver may invoke routines in the original calling program. Drivers are hardware dependent and operating-system-specific. They usually provide the interrupt handling required for any necessary asynchronous time-dependent hardware interface.

artifacts.name: Computer Enclosure
artifacts.definition: A part providing protection of computer equipment against certain external influences and protects against direct contact.

artifacts.name: Pointer
artifacts.definition: In computer science, a pointer is a programming language object, whose value refers to (or "points to") another value stored elsewhere in the computer memory using its memory address. A pointer references a location in memory, and obtaining the value stored at that location is known as dereferencing the pointer. As an analogy, a page number in a book's index could be considered a pointer to the corresponding page; dereferencing such a pointer would be done by flipping to the page with the given page number.

artifacts.name: Application Configuration
artifacts.definition: Information used to configure the parameters and initial settings for an application.

artifacts.name: Process Segment
artifacts.definition: Process segments are distinct partitions of the memory space of a running process.  Heap, data, code, and stack segments are examples of process segments.

artifacts.name: Stack Frame
artifacts.definition: A machine-dependent and application-binary-dependent (ABI-dependent) data structure containing subroutine state information including the arguments passed into the routine, the return address back to the routine's caller, and space for local variables of the routine.

artifacts.name: Control Flow Policy
artifacts.definition: A control flow policy is a subset of the possible control flow transfers computed from a program's control flow graph. It defines only the expected and allowed control flow transfers and is enforced by control flow integrity.

artifacts.name: Call Stack
artifacts.definition: In computer science, a call stack is a stack data structure that stores information about the active subroutines of a computer program. This kind of stack is also known as an execution stack, program stack, control stack, run-time stack, or machine stack, and is often shortened to just "the stack". Although maintenance of the call stack is important for the proper functioning of most software, the details are normally hidden and automatic in high-level programming languages. Many computer instruction sets provide special instructions for manipulating stacks.

artifacts.name: Shadow Stack
artifacts.definition: A shadow stack is a mechanism for protecting a procedure's stored return address, such as from a stack buffer overflow. The shadow stack itself is a second, separate stack that "shadows" the program call stack. In the function prologue, a function stores its return address to both the call stack and the shadow stack. In the function epilogue, a function loads the return address from both the call stack and the shadow stack, and then compares them. If the two records of the return address differ, then an attack is detected.

artifacts.name: Control Flow Graph
artifacts.definition: A control flow graph is a representation of all possible control flow transfers within a program, typically computed at compile-time or link-time, including calls, jumps, and returns. The control flow graph can be used to compute a control flow policy that permits only the expected control flow transfers during process execution via control flow integrity mechanisms.

artifacts.name: Memory Address
artifacts.definition: In computing, a memory address is a reference to a specific memory location used at various levels by software and hardware.

artifacts.name: RPC Network Traffic
artifacts.definition: RPC network traffic is network traffic related to remote procedure calls between network nodes..This includes only network traffic conforming to a standard RPC protocol; not custom protocols.

artifacts.name: Intranet IPC Network Traffic
artifacts.definition: Intranet IPC network traffic is network traffic that does not cross a given network's boundaries and uses a standard inter-process communication (IPC) networking protocol.

artifacts.name: Network Traffic
artifacts.definition: Network traffic or data traffic is the data, or alternatively the amount of data, moving across a network at a given point of time.  Network data in computer networks is mostly encapsulated in network packets, which provide the load in the network.

artifacts.name: Outbound Internet Network Traffic
artifacts.definition: Outbound internet network traffic is network traffic on an outgoing connection initiated from a host within a network to a host outside the network.

artifacts.name: Outbound Internet DNS Lookup Traffic
artifacts.definition: Outbound internet DNS lookup traffic is network traffic using the DNS protocol on an outgoing connection initiated from a host within a network to a host outside the network.

artifacts.name: DNS Lookup
artifacts.definition: A Domain Name System (DNS) lookup is a record returned from a DNS resolver after querying a DNS name server.  Typically considered an A or AAAA record, where a domain name is resolved to an IPv4 or IPv6 address, respectively.

artifacts.name: File Transfer Network Traffic
artifacts.definition: File transfer network traffic is network traffic related to file transfers between network nodes. This includes only network traffic conforming to standard file transfer protocols, not custom transfer protocols.

artifacts.name: OT Device Firmware Command
artifacts.definition: Interact with the software responsible for low-level control of the system.

artifacts.name: OT Network Traffic
artifacts.definition: Network traffic generated by operational technology devices, e.g., programmable logic controllers.

artifacts.name: Inbound Internet Network Traffic
artifacts.definition: Inbound internet traffic is network traffic from a host outside a given network initiated on an incoming connection to a host inside that network.

artifacts.name: Intranet Administrative Network Traffic
artifacts.definition: Intranet administrative network traffic is administrative network traffic that does not cross a given network's boundaries and uses a standard administrative protocol.

artifacts.name: Intranet Network Traffic
artifacts.definition: Intranet network traffic is network traffic traversing that does not traverse a given network's boundaries.

artifacts.name: Certificate File
artifacts.definition: A file containing a digital certificate. In cryptography, a public key certificate (also known as a digital certificate or identity certificate) is an electronic document used to prove the ownership of a public key. The certificate includes information about the key, information about its owner's identity, and the digital signature of an entity that has verified the certificate's contents are correct. If the signature is valid, and the person examining the certificate trusts the signer, then they know they can use that key to communicate with its owner.

artifacts.name: Email
artifacts.definition: An email, or email message, is a document that is sent between computer users across computer networks.

artifacts.name: Local Resource Access
artifacts.definition: Ephemeral digital artifact comprising a request of a local resource and any response from that resource.

artifacts.name: Database Query
artifacts.definition: A specific query expressed in SQL, SPARQL, or similar language against a database.

artifacts.name: Script Application Process
artifacts.definition: A script application process is an application process interpreting an executable script.

artifacts.name: Create Process
definition: A process spawn refers to a function that loads and executes a new child process.The current process may wait for the child to terminate or may continue to execute asynchronously. Creating a new subprocess requires enough memory in which both the child process and the current program can execute. There is a family of spawn functions in DOS, inherited by Microsoft Windows. There is also a different family of spawn functions in an optional extension of the POSIX standards.  Fork-exec is another technique combining two Unix system calls, which can effect a process spawn.

artifacts.name: Process
artifacts.definition: A process is an instance of a computer program that is being executed. It contains the program code and its current activity. Depending on the operating system (OS), a process may be made up of multiple threads of execution that execute instructions concurrently. A computer program is a passive collection of instructions, while a process is the actual execution of those instructions. Several processes may be associated with the same program; for example, opening up several instances of the same program often means more than one process is being executed.

artifacts.name: Process Tree
artifacts.definition: A process tree is a tree structure representation of parent-child relationships established via process spawn operations.

artifacts.name: System Call
artifacts.definition: A system call is the programmatic way in which a computer program requests a service from the kernel of the operating system it is executed on. This may include hardware-related services (for example, accessing a hard disk drive), creation and execution of new processes, and communication with integral kernel services such as process scheduling. System calls provide an essential interface between a process and the operating system.

artifacts.name: Create File
artifacts.definition: System call to create a new file on a file system. Some operating systems implement this functionality as part of their d3f:OpenFile system call.

artifacts.name: Process Code Segment
artifacts.definition: A process code segment, also known as a text segment or simply as text, is a portion of the program's virtual address space that contains executable instructions and corresponds to the loaded image code segment. Includes additional sections such as an import table.

artifacts.name: Digital Camera
artifacts.definition: An optical instrument that can capture an image. A digital camera that captures photographs in digital memory.

artifacts.name: Proximity Sensor
artifacts.definition: A sensor able to detect the presence of nearby objects without any physical contact.

artifacts.name: Motion Detector
artifacts.definition: An electrical device that utilizes a sensor to detect nearby motion.

artifacts.name: Electronic Combination Lock
artifacts.definition: A system comprised of an automatic door closer on the door, an input device, a controlling device, and a lock, usually mechanical, which is released or activated when the correct combination is entered or correct token is presented.

artifacts.name: Executable File
artifacts.definition: In computing, executable code or an executable file or executable program, sometimes simply an executable, causes a computer "to perform indicated tasks according to encoded instructions," as opposed to a data file that must be parsed by a program to be meaningful. These instructions are traditionally machine code instructions for a physical CPU. However, in a more general sense, a file containing instructions (such as bytecode) for a software interpreter may also be considered executable; even a scripting language source file may therefore be considered executable in this sense. The exact interpretation depends upon the use; while the term often refers only to machine code files, in the context of protection against computer viruses all files which cause potentially hazardous instruction

artifacts.name: Domain User Account
artifacts.definition: A domain user account in Microsoft Windows (2000) defines that user's access to a logical group of network objects (computers, users, devices) that share the same Active Directory databases; that is, a user's access to a domain.

artifacts.name: Authentication
artifacts.definition: A request-response comprising a user credential presentation to a system and a verification response.

artifacts.name: Authorization
artifacts.definition: Authorization is the function of specifying access rights to resources related to information security and computer security in general and to access control in particular. More formally, "to authorize" is to define an access policy. For example, human resources staff is normally authorized to access employee records and this policy is usually formalized as access control rules in a computer system. During operation, the system uses the access control rules to decide whether access requests from (authenticated) consumers shall be approved (granted) or disapproved (rejected). Resources include individual files or an item's data, computer programs, computer devices and functionality provided by computer applications. Examples of consumers are computer users, computer program

artifacts.name: Web Resource Access
artifacts.definition: Ephemeral digital artifact comprising a request of a network resource and any response from that network resource using a standard web protocol.

artifacts.name: Local User Account
artifacts.definition: A user account on a given host is a local user account for that specific host.

artifacts.name: Resource Access
artifacts.definition: Ephemeral digital artifact comprising a request of a resource and any response from that resource.

artifacts.name: URL
artifacts.definition: A Uniform Resource Locator (URL), commonly informally termed a web address (a term which is not defined identically) is a reference to a web resource that specifies its location on a computer network and a mechanism for retrieving it.A URL is a specific type of Uniform Resource Identifier (URI), although many people use the two terms interchangeably. A URL implies the means to access an indicated resource, which is not true of every URI. URLs occur most commonly to reference web pages (http), but are also used for file transfer (ftp), email (mailto), database access (JDBC), and many other applications.

artifacts.name: IP Address
artifacts.definition: An Internet Protocol address (IP address) is a numerical label assigned to each device connected to a computer network that uses the Internet Protocol for communication.An IP address serves two main functions: host or network interface identification and location addressing.
